# 艺术·音乐·文学 {.unnumbered}



> 本主题共 6 篇语境短文。每篇把一批旧词织进一个场景：**左栏**读短文（目标词加粗），**右栏**常驻该篇生词释义，可先猜后对照。



### A Long Night of Art, Music, and Story

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
The small gallery smelled of **sumi** ink and old varnish. On the far wall hung a **stele** rubbing mounted behind glass, its **tone** somewhere between ash and charcoal — a shade the curator called **noir** without irony. Beside it, a row of **delft** tiles arranged in a frieze carried a recurring **motif** of waves and ships, each **carved** by hand generations ago. A glass cabinet displayed a single **prunt**-studded goblet, the melted bead of decoration catching the light like a trapped insect. In the corner, a placard identified the instrument on the pedestal as a **qanon**, its strings long silent.

The evening's programme began with a **bop** quartet — no announcement, no **debut** fanfare, just four musicians taking their places and counting in. The **bass** settled into a low pulse while the **flute** climbed above it, the two lines forming a loose **duet** before the full **choir** of sound arrived. A single **bell** struck once from the back of the hall; whether it was **cast** iron or bronze no one knew, but the ring held the room. The recording that followed was deliberately **mono**, played through a single speaker to match the decade it came from, a **tune** so familiar the audience hummed without realising it. The **tenor** soloist entered halfway through the **canto**, steadying the **barre** of the phrase as if resting a palm on a dancer's rail.

Later, in the reading room, a writer introduced her new collection. The stories moved between **genre** with ease — **fable** one moment, **satirical** sketch the next, with one long piece that had the cold palette of **noir** fiction. She read a passage in which a **bard** performs at a provincial court, a **clown** hovering at the edge of the scene for **jest** that never quite lands. The prose had its own **motif**: a repeated image of a **gig** played in an empty street, music leaking out of a **mono** speaker nailed above a door. The **elegy** near the end of the set silenced the room completely, its **tone** shifting from wry distance to something that asked more of the listener than a simple **tune** ever could.

### Between the Gallery and the Concert Hall

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
The old artist sat beneath an **antique** lamp, rolling a **crayon** between her fingers before pressing it to the sketchpad. The **sketch** began simply — a doorway, a **statue** half-buried in ivy — rendered in **pastel** blues and creams that seemed to breathe in the soft light. Around the figure she pressed small **motifs**: a vine, a key, a bird mid-flight. The image was **iconic** already, the kind that becomes a **legend** in its own neighbourhood. To one side she had pinned a **parody** of Rodin clipped from a magazine, a reminder that great work and **satire** share the same root: the refusal to look away. She liked to **doodle** in the margins while she thought, little spirals and faces that no one would ever **depict** in a serious review, yet which held more of her true voice than anything she had tried to **endite** in words.

In the next room, the chamber group was warming up. The **fiddle** player drew a long open note; the **viola** answered a third below; then a **treble** line from the violin curled upward like smoke. They ran a **medley** of sea-**ballad**s — **melody** following **melody** in loose **unison**, each one a **stanza** of sound complete in itself. The **reggae**-inflected bridge the arranger had spliced into the middle was a small shock, a tonal **trope** that should not have worked but did, the way a sudden **simile** rescues a flat sentence. Through the old **stereo** in the corridor the **finale** of last night's recording played back, the **rhymes** of bow-stroke and breath still audible beneath the hiss of the tape.

Downstairs, a young critic was writing the **sequel** to his first pamphlet — a piece of **sitcom**-length **satire** aimed at the art world's habit of calling every **acrobat** with a spray-can a visionary. He paused, listening to the music drift down the stairwell, and for a moment forgot what he had been so eager to mock.

### A Gallery Evening, an Open Stage, a Quiet Studio

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
The **vintage** poster in the lobby announced a **Baroque** ensemble concert, its **cursive** lettering pressed in **italics** across aged paper. Inside the gallery, a **replica** of a medieval archer's bow hung beside a bronze figure mid-draw — the museum's small nod to the history of **archery** before the main exhibits began. Visitors moved past a glass case of **origami** cranes, then paused at a panel of **macrame** wall-hangings, their knotted fringes catching the low light like a kind of **crochet** translated into rope.

In the adjoining hall, a curator had chosen to **exhibit** three pieces together: an oil painting of a **masquer** frozen mid-bow at a Renaissance ball, a stone **carving** of a lute player worn smooth by centuries, and a small **rosette** medallion cast in silver. The arrangement was no **charade** — each object spoke to the others, and the **sonance** of the space itself seemed to deepen as visitors slowed down. A **lyrical** passage from Voltaire's **Candide** was printed on the far wall, the lines about naive wonder in an indifferent world still landing with full force. Beside it, a footnote mentioned **Laertes** — that other literary figure undone by the gap between appearance and truth.

Downstairs, a live program was already running. A **soprano** stepped to the microphone, and for a few bars the room went completely still; every syllable was **audible** even in the back rows. A **bassoon** entered beneath her, anchoring the **cadence** before a recorded loop of **gamelan** textures washed in from the speakers — an unexpected pairing that somehow held. Between sets, a young poet read an **excerpt** from a longer work, and the host had to **compose** herself before introducing the next act: a **karaoke** segment built entirely from operatic arias, absurd and earnest in equal measure. A documentary crew filmed everything, planning to **portray** the evening as a study in how **erotica**, sacred music, and folk craft could share the same room without apology. On a side table, handmade **puppets** from a local theatre workshop waited their turn, an **allegory** in felt and wire for whatever the night still wanted to say.

### The Night Before the Premiere

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
A **drumroll** shook the velvet curtains as the **ensemble** gathered backstage, nerves crackling in the dim corridor. The director, a two-time **laureate** of the national arts prize, paced the wings clutching his **playbook** — annotated in red, its margins filled with the kind of **literary** instincts that turn a script into something alive. Tonight's production was built around an original **symphony**, and every player had spent the past month learning to navigate its **diatonic** passages, coaxing melody out of what had first sounded like **monotone** repetition. Earlier in the week the lead soprano had nearly lost her slot at the **audition**, her voice turning **screechy** under the pressure of the upper register, but by Thursday she had found her footing and earned her place beside the countertenor — a modern echo of the Baroque **castrato** tradition, his rare timbre cutting cleanly through the brass.

The **overture** opened in restraint, a single **drumbeat** grounding the hall before the strings bloomed outward. On the walls of the foyer, the production designers had chosen to **decorate** every surface with care: framed **ceramics** from the collection of a retired art dealer stood beside glass cases of polished **antiques**, and a cluster of **statuary** — **rendered** in pale limestone — watched the arriving audience from the alcove. A long **epigraph** had been **freehand** lettered in ink directly onto the plaster above the main entrance: *Music begins where words end.* The choice was unmistakably **symbolic**, grounding a modern evening in a lineage that stretched back to the ancient **rhapsode** chanting Homer by firelight.

When the **postlude** finally faded and the hall exhaled, the **splendor** of the night settled over everyone like a held breath released at last. The director had written a brief **prologue** for the programme notes, describing how months of **rehearse** had transformed raw material into something **animated** — breathing, urgent, present. The sound crew rewound the **cassette** of the dress rehearsal, archiving it alongside the earlier digital mix. Outside, critics already opening their laptops reached for the **esthetic** vocabulary they reserve for work that earns it: shaped, considered, whole. And on the stage, still lit by a single follow spot, the ensemble stood in the **overture**'s echo — each of them an **ornament** in the larger structure, each of them, for this one night, more than enough.

### A Night at the Arts Festival

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
The evening opened with a series of living **tableaux** — performers frozen mid-gesture beneath amber light, each pose a **vignette** of some forgotten myth. The **aesthetic** of the whole festival leaned toward the ornate: every surface **chromatic**, every detail deliberate.

Backstage, the energy was the opposite of stillness. A **ballerina** stretched at the barre while a percussionist tested his **drumstick** against a practice pad. Nearby, a child prodigy ran scales on a **xylophone**, its bright tones cutting through the hum of a **harmonica** someone was warming up in the corner. A performer in a folk trio clicked her **castanets** in a slow, meditative rhythm, and the player of a **concertina** squeezed a long, reedy chord that hung in the air.

The **rehearsal** had gone badly that afternoon. The director felt the ensemble's **rendering** of the second act was **contrived** — too careful, too much **imitation** of the original production and not enough life of its own. He wanted them to **improvise**, to find something genuine. "Stop trying to be **harmonious** on purpose," he said. "Just play." The **impromptu** run-through that followed was rough but alive. A wandering **fantasist** of a composer, watching from the wings, began to **delineate** a new arrangement on the back of a **paperback** anthology of contemporary verse — the only paper he had.

The festival's star attraction was a **marionette** show whose **portrayal** of jealousy had drawn comparisons to Greek tragedy. Critics argued whether the **depiction** was profound or merely **grotesque**; the crowds didn't care either way. It had become the **smash hit** of the season. A reviewer called it "an **exquisite** **caricature** of human longing" — the kind of line that looks sharp in print but dissolves under thinking. The show's lead designer, interviewed in a short **animation** segment for the festival program, said only that she had tried to **sculpture** the puppets so their stillness felt like held breath.

By midnight the stages were dark, and the **anthology** on the composer's lap had thirty new margin notes.
:::

### The Archive Room

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
In the city's oldest concert hall, a **documentary** crew had spent three days filming what they hoped would be a **prizewinning** portrait of the venue's century-long life. The **protagonist** of their film was not a person but a place — its worn oak floors, its dusty **terracotta** friezes, and the glass cabinet in the lobby where a yellowed **sketchbook**, once belonging to the hall's founding architect, lay open to a drawing of the original stage. Beside it sat a small **tambourine**, said to have been played at the inaugural concert in 1902. The crew's director had wanted to **fictionalize** parts of the story, but the archivist refused; this was **historiography**, not drama — every claim had to be **bibliographic**, traceable to a primary source.

On the afternoon of the third day, the hall's resident **accompanist** sat at the Bösendorfer and worked through the evening soloist's **repertoire**, marking tempos in pencil. A **disc jockey** from the local radio station had arrived to record a short feature, his equipment stacked **rhythmically** in road cases along the corridor. The two nodded at each other across the lobby — an unlikely **counterpoint**, analog keys against digital decks. The director, watching from the doorway, began to **orchestrate** the afternoon's shots in her mind: she would open on the **calligraphy** of the concert program — all copperplate, no **typographical** compromise — then cut to the archivist's hand, whose lifelong practice of **chirography** had produced thirty years of catalog cards in a script that looked almost **allegorical**, each letter leaning forward as if it meant something beyond itself.

The evening's program included a short work that critics had called **blockbuster** in reach if not in length — a tone poem the composer had built, with full **poetic license**, around a scene he refused to explain. Some listeners found the middle passage nearly **pornographic** in its emotional exposure; others called it simply brave. Before the performance began, a young actor hired to **impersonate** a nineteenth-century impresario for a lobby tableau adjusted his coat under the **Michelangelo** reproduction someone had hung above the fireplace — a small joke, or perhaps an aspiration. The documentary camera, already rolling, caught all of it.
:::
